meta.title: Who really said "I Was the Toast of Two Continents: Greenland and Australia"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Dorothy Parker, probably — but not in these words. The earliest version, from 1956, names Asia and Africa. Greenland and Australia came later.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I Was the Toast of Two Continents: Greenland and Australia'?
meta.ogDescription: The joke is Parker’s, on the earliest evidence. The continents are not: a 1956 column has her saying "Asia and Africa."

answer.label: Parker’s joke — but the continents were Asia and Africa
answer.authorDates: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and short-story writer
answer.sourceLine: The earliest known printing is a syndicated column by Leonard Lyons ↗, carried in the Dallas Morning News of 15 October 1956, and it reads: “Dorothy Parker said: I once was the toast of two continents, Asia and Africa.” Both of those are continents, which is the point — the “Greenland and Australia” form, in which one of the two is an island, does not appear until around 1970. Quote Investigator ↗ gives Parker the credit “for now” because she is named in that first citation, while noting that Bennett Cerf ↗ believed Frank Sullivan ↗ said it first.
answer.confidenceText: Right person, drifted wording — and even the person is credited only on the earliest available citation.

source.excerpt: Dorothy Parker said: “I once was the toast of two continents, Asia and Africa.”
trail: Quote Investigator’s article ↗ is the anchor. It identifies the earliest instance as Leonard Lyons’s column in the Dallas Morning News, 15 October 1956, in the “Asia and Africa” wording, and states that “since Parker is mentioned in the first cite she receives the credit for now.”

The joke works by twisting a stock phrase. QI shows “the toast of two continents” in its ordinary sense in a 1933 newspaper tribute to the jockey Tod Sloan, famous in both America and Britain. Parker’s version keeps the grammar and swaps in two continents nobody tours — the deflation is the whole gag.

The mutation is documented, not inferred. QI records the “Greenland and Australia” form appearing by 1970 in John Keats’s biography You Might As Well Live: The Life and Times of Dorothy Parker. Greenland is not a continent, which is the objection that prompted the original enquiry to QI — and QI’s answer is that the funnier, wronger version is the one that survived.

The credit is not secure even for Parker. In a 1971 column Bennett Cerf ↗ wrote that both Robert Benchley ↗ and Parker had been credited with the line, “but I think it was Frank Sullivan ↗ who said it first.” All three sat at the Algonquin Round Table ↗ in the 1920s, yet the earliest citation anyone has found is from the 1950s — a thirty-year gap that no source closes.
source.excerptNote: That is Quote Investigator’s transcription ↗ of the 1956 Lyons column, the earliest printing located. The version this page is titled for — “Greenland and Australia” — is a later reshaping, and it is the reshaping that made the joke famous, so we keep it as the headline while recording what the source actually says.

author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.heading: About Dorothy Parker
author.metaLine: 1893–1967 · American poet, critic and short-story writer
author.bio: Dorothy Parker (born Dorothy Rothschild, 22 August 1893 – 7 June 1967) was an American poet, critic and short-story writer and a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table. Self-deprecation was as much her register as the put-down, and a joke about being famous in exactly the wrong places is entirely in character. That same reputation is why so many unsourced wisecracks end up on her — and why Wikiquote heads her Misattributed section ↗ with a standing warning about it.

misattribution.heading: What is actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited on this one — the earliest source really does name Parker. What has gone wrong is the sentence itself, plus a genuine uncertainty about the 1920s that no citation reaches back far enough to settle.

items.why: The 1956 printing transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ reads “Asia and Africa.” The Greenland/Australia form is not recorded until about 1970. It is the better joke and the worse geography, and it is the one that survived.
In 1971 Bennett Cerf ↗ wrote that Benchley and Parker had both been credited “but I think it was Frank Sullivan ↗ who said it first.” QI records this without resolving it; neither do we.

The line is usually told as Round Table lore, but the earliest citation anyone has produced is from 1956 — roughly thirty years after the fact. That gap is the reason this page is filed as disputed rather than verified.

misattribution.truthLine: Parker is the best-supported author and the words are not quite hers: she named Asia and Africa, and someone else swapped in Greenland and Australia — see Quote Investigator’s trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: “The toast of two continents” was press-agent boilerplate for a performer who had conquered both America and Europe. Parker’s joke is a demolition of that phrase: keep the format, keep the boast, and fill it with two places that confer no glamour whatsoever.

Which two places is a matter of taste, and taste has revised the line. Asia and Africa are continents and the sentence is literally correct; Greenland and Australia are funnier because one of them is not a continent at all. The version that spread is the one that is wrong on purpose — or wrong by accident, and kept because it landed better.
detailsBody: It is worth being clear about what this page is and is not claiming. It is not claiming Parker never made this joke; the earliest source we have says she did. It is claiming that the exact sentence in the headline is not the sentence anyone recorded her saying, and that the thirty-year gap between the Algonquin years and the first citation leaves real room for Bennett Cerf’s alternative.

That is why the page is filed as disputed while still crediting Parker. The alternative — printing “Greenland and Australia” under her name as a verified quotation — would assert a wording no source supports, which is precisely the error this site exists to correct.
context.pull: The version that spread is the one that is wrong on purpose.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator gives the earliest instance as Leonard Lyons’s column in the Dallas Morning News, 15 October 1956, worded "I once was the toast of two continents, Asia and Africa"; records the Greenland/Australia form by 1970 in John Keats’s biography; quotes Bennett Cerf in 1971 saying he thinks Frank Sullivan said it first; cites a 1933 Milwaukee Journal use of "the toast of two continents" about the jockey Tod Sloan; and concludes Parker "receives the credit for now".
Wikipedia gives Dorothy Parker as born Dorothy Rothschild, 22 August 1893, died 7 June 1967, an American poet, writer and critic.
Wikiquote’s Dorothy Parker page does not carry this line, and heads its Misattributed section with a warning that a great many misquotations are attributed to her.
Wikipedia has a biography of the syndicated columnist Leonard Lyons.
